To reify something means to take an abstract idea, concept, or relationship — something that doesn't physically exist as a "thing" — and treat it as if it were a concrete, real, solid, independent object in the world.

The simplest way to put it: reifying = turning a thought into a "thing."
A Simple Analogy to Lock It In

Imagine you and your friends have a running joke. It's not a physical object. It's just a pattern of behaviour and shared memory between people. It lives in interactions.

Now imagine someone says, "The joke has a life of its own now" or "The joke is taking over our friend group." They're treating "the joke" as if it has agency, weight, and independent existence — as if it were an entity that can act on its own.

That's reification. You took something that only exists as a social, mental, or relational phenomenon and mentally solidified it into a thing.

The world is full of abstractions — things that exist only as ideas, patterns, processes, or relationships, not as physical objects you can touch. Examples:

  • Justice
  • The economy
  • Love
  • Society
  • Race
  • Time
  • Democracy

None of these is a brick you can hold. They're complex, shifting, human-made constructs or processes.

When you reify them, you start speaking about — and more importantly, thinking about — them as though they are fixed, independent, concrete things with their own properties, their own existence, sometimes even their own will.

Example 1 — "The market decided."
Markets aren't single decision-makers. A market is millions of individual human choices, behaviours, social norms, power structures, and historical forces all interacting. But when someone says "the market decided," they collapse all that complexity into a single, concrete-seeming entity that has made a decision. The market has been reified.

Example 2 — "Society is to blame."
Society isn't a person or an object. It's a web of relationships, institutions, and shared norms among people. But when we say "society is to blame," we treat it like a unified agent that has done something. Society has been reified.

Example 3 — "Time is running out."
Time is a concept, a measurement, a dimension of experience. It doesn't literally run. But we speak of it as if it were a substance being depleted from a container. Time has been reified.

Example 4 — "Race determines outcomes."
Race is a social and historical construct — a category humans invented and assigned meaning to. It has no biological solidity. But when people treat racial categories as fixed, natural, self-evidently real properties that people simply have, they are reifying race. The social construction has been turned into a "thing."
The Critical/Philosophical Dimension (Where the Word Is Most Powerful)

Reification becomes a genuinely important concept when it causes harm or hides truth. Here's why:

When you reify something that is actually a human-made construct or a social arrangement, you can make it seem:

  • Natural — as though it has always existed and must exist
  • Inevitable — as though it cannot be changed
  • Objective — as though it exists outside of human choices and history

This is dangerous because it strips away agency. If "the economy" is a real, solid thing operating on its own laws, then humans can't change it — they can only react to it. But if you de-reify that thought and remember that the economy is a set of human-created rules, institutions, and choices, then suddenly it becomes something that can be redesigned.

This is why thinkers in philosophy, sociology, and critical theory use "reify" as a concept for exposing a mental trap: we forget that we built the cage, and so we stop thinking we can leave it.

To reify a social construct is to forget its history — and forgetting its history makes it feel eternal.

Not all uses of "reify" carry this critical weight. In computer science, to reify something means to make an abstract concept into an explicit, first-class object within a system so that it can be manipulated and used directly.

For example, in programming, a "query" is a conceptual request for data. If a language reifies queries — turns them into actual objects in the code — then programmers can store them, pass them around, and operate on them like any other object. Here, reification is simply useful and practical. There's no criticism implied.

So in technical contexts, to reify = to make something abstract into something you can directly work with.
How to Recognise Reification in the Wild

Ask yourself: Is this person treating an idea or a process as though it were a fixed, concrete, self-existing thing?

Signals to watch for:

  • An abstraction is given agency ("the institution decided," "nature wants," "capitalism demands")
  • A process is spoken about as a static object (instead of "people discriminating," someone says "discrimination is just how things are")
  • A constructed category is treated as a natural kind — something that exists in the world independently of human thought and history
  • Something changeable is spoken of as inevitable

When you spot these, you're likely watching reification in action.

To reify is to take something abstract — an idea, a relationship, a social construct, a process — and treat it as though it is a concrete, fixed, independent thing that simply exists in the world.

The word is used critically (to expose a way of thinking that hides human agency and historical contingency) and technically (to make an abstract concept usable and manipulable in a system). Either way, the core action is the same: turning an abstraction into a "thing."
